question: In children who have K-wire fixation of a supracondylar fracture, does the operation note state when the wires will come out?
why: Missing wire-removal plans cause lost-to-follow-up wires and extra clinic visits. Corpus supracondylar audits measure nerve checks and 2 mm wires [1640, 1232], not this item; no audit in corpus.

standard.source: BOAST Supracondylar Fractures of the Humerus in Children (October 2020), standard 12
standard.wording: The operating surgeon should determine and document the need for post-operative radiographs and anticipated time of wire removal.

pass: Operation note records the anticipated time of wire removal (e.g. '3–4 weeks, in clinic'). The need for post-operative X-rays is collected as a secondary item.
population: Children under 16 with a supracondylar humerus fracture fixed with K-wires. Exclude open reductions for vascular exploration if the note is written by vascular surgery only.
sample: 40 consecutive cases from the theatre system, going back up to 18 months.
data_source: Theatre system (case list, date); electronic operation note (wire plan, X-ray plan, grade of author); clinic letters (actual removal date).

More than 1 week after the planned time

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add two mandatory drop-down fields to the paediatric K-wire operation note template: 'wire removal at __ weeks' and 'post-op X-ray: yes/no'.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 20–40 consecutive cases after the template goes live, same template.
close_loop: Present at trauma and orthopaedic governance and the paediatric fracture clinic team. If it works, keep the fields mandatory and add to the unit's supracondylar pathway.
evidence: [1483] Royal London trauma: post-operative instructions → 100% (smart electronic operation note with drop-downs)
[2256] general surgery: overall operation note compliance <80% → >98% (electronic proforma built with IT)
[1232] Stevenage supracondylar: information booklet alone gave mixed gains and time to theatre regressed (education only)
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from theatre system and EPR

question: When a medial K-wire is used for a child's supracondylar fracture, does the operation note record how the ulnar nerve was protected?
why: Iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury is a known risk of medial wires and a medicolegal issue. Corpus audits count crossed wires [1543] but none check the op-note record of ulnar nerve protection; no audit in corpus.

standard.source: BOAST Supracondylar Fractures of the Humerus in Children (October 2020), standard 6
standard.wording: When a medial wire is used, techniques to avoid ulnar nerve injury should be employed and recorded on the operation note.

pass: Operation note names a technique (e.g. mini-open medial incision, elbow extended when the medial wire goes in, nerve palpated and held back).
population: Children under 16 with supracondylar fixation that includes at least one medial-entry wire (from op note or intra-operative image). Exclude lateral-only constructs.
sample: All medial-wire cases over the last 24 months (expect 20–40 in a trauma unit; pool across 2 sites if fewer).
data_source: Theatre system; operation note; intra-operative fluoroscopy images on PACS (to confirm medial wire); post-op clinic letters (ulnar nerve status).

question: When a child's supracondylar fracture is fixed at night, is the urgent reason for night surgery documented?
why: Night operating on children carries more risk and is often avoidable. Corpus audits measure time to theatre [1232] and one noted night operating in passing [1211]; none measure the documented indication.

standard.source: BOAST Supracondylar Fractures of the Humerus in Children (October 2020), standard 2
standard.wording: Surgical management should be carried out on the day of injury. Night-time operating is not necessary unless there are indications for urgent surgery which should be documented.

pass: For a case with knife-to-skin between 22:00 and 07:59, the notes or booking record an urgent indication (absent radial pulse, impaired hand perfusion, open injury or threatened skin, or other stated reason).
population: Children under 16 with supracondylar fixation starting 22:00–07:59. Exclude cases done in the day.
sample: All night-time cases over the last 24 months (expect 20–40); also record total cases to give the night-time rate.
data_source: Theatre system (knife-to-skin time); emergency theatre booking form; ED and orthopaedic clerking; operation note.

question: Do children with a suspected limb fracture and moderate or severe pain get analgesia within 30 minutes of arrival?

standard.source: RCEM Pain in Children QIP 2021/22, standard 2 (fundamental)
standard.wording: 2. Administration of analgesia to patients in severe pain F = within 30 minutes D = within 20 minutes 2. Administration of analgesia to patients in moderate pain F = within 30 minutes D = within 20 minutes

pass: First analgesic given within 30 minutes of arrival (or triage, if earlier) when the pain score is moderate (4–7) or severe (7–10).
population: Children under 16 with a suspected long-bone limb fracture and a recorded moderate or severe pain score. Exclude those given analgesia pre-hospital and in no pain at triage.
sample: 40 consecutive children over the last 1–2 months.
data_source: ED EPR (arrival and triage times, pain score); drug chart/e-prescribing administration time; ambulance record.

change: Add a '12-month infection review with X-ray' field to the discharge letter template and an outpatient outcome code that blocks discharge from clinic before 12 months.
reaudit: At 12 months, prospectively on children diagnosed after the change, same template; meanwhile check clinic bookings at 3 months.
close_loop: Present to the paediatric orthopaedic team and outpatient managers. If it works, keep the outcome code and discharge field.
evidence: [1337] UCLH: 0% → 92.9% (mandatory discharge template field)
[1527] Aberdeen: dedicated acute clinic cut time to surgery from mean 14 to 6 months (system change)
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from clinic letters and PACS

question: Is every child treated for a slipped upper femoral epiphysis discussed at a documented regional peer review meeting?
why: SUFE is rare and life-changing, and DGH surgeons pin few. The corpus has no SUFE audit at all; BSCOS now lists SUFE for peer review.

standard.source: BSCOS Best Practice in Children's Trauma & Orthopaedics in the UK (November 2025), Section 3 Key Points: Life Changing Injuries
standard.wording: Specific paediatric injuries that could have potentially life-changing results should be discussed at PRMs. These should include amongst others: open fractures, pelvic fractures, femoral neck fractures, Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis (SUFE), lower limb physeal fractures, intra-articular fractures and pathological fractures or fractures occurring in children with underlying musculoskeletal conditions

pass: Minutes of a regional or network peer review meeting (or MDT) record discussion of the case.
population: Children treated (operatively or not) for SUFE at the unit. Exclude cases treated only at the tertiary centre after transfer.
sample: All cases over the last 36 months (expect 15–40 in a DGH; pool with network units if fewer).
data_source: Theatre system and coding (SUFE procedures); peer review/MDT minutes; clinic letters (stability, symptom duration).

reaudit: At 6–12 months: all cases since the change, same template.
close_loop: Present at the paediatric trauma network/ODN meeting. If it works, extend auto-listing to the other BSCOS life-changing injuries.
evidence: [1281] Wythenshawe: trauma meeting cases documented 64% → 88% (structured proforma)
[1692] Wythenshawe: 64% → 84% (EPR trauma meeting proforma)
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from theatre coding and meeting minutes

question: Do babies with a screen-positive newborn hip result have their hip ultrasound between 4 and 6 weeks of age?
why: Late scans delay harness treatment for DDH. Corpus has an old breech-referral audit [1435] and an Irish programme review with no loop [1613]; no audit of the 2024 NIPE timing standard.

standard.source: NHS NIPE screening standards, NIPE-S03 (valid for data collected from 1 April 2024)
standard.wording: The proportion of babies with a screen positive newborn hip result who attend for ultrasound scan of the hips within the designated timescale.

pass: Babies born at 34+0 weeks or later scanned at ≥4 weeks 0 days and ≤6 weeks 0 days of age (42 days); babies born before 34+0 weeks scanned at 38+0 to 40+0 weeks corrected age. Thresholds: acceptable ≥90%, achievable ≥95%.
population: Babies with a screen-positive newborn hip result (abnormal Barlow/Ortolani or a national hip risk factor). Exclude babies who died before the appointment and 'clicky hips'.
sample: 40 consecutive screen-positive babies over the last 3–6 months.
data_source: S4N (screen result, risk factor); RIS (scan date); birth record (gestation, date of birth).

template.note: Local study code; key kept separately on a trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: At the newborn check, the NIPE practitioner books the hip scan directly into a RIS slot dated for day 28–35, and the date is printed on the parent's discharge letter.
reaudit: Wk 13–14 on babies born after the change, same template.
close_loop: Present to the local screening board, neonatal and radiology teams. If it works, embed booking at the newborn check in the local NIPE SOP.
evidence: [1435] Glasgow neonatal: breech babies referred 56% → 76% (proforma at the newborn check)
[1613] Irish DDH programme: 26% referred to clinic; timing reported without a loop
effort: ~10 min per 10 babies from S4N and RIS

question: Are infants with a screen-positive hip at the 6 to 8 week check seen by a paediatric orthopaedic surgeon by 10 weeks of age?
why: Late-found DDH needs fast specialist review because harness success falls with age. No audit in corpus.

standard.source: NHS NIPE screening programme handbook (updated October 2025), section 14.11
standard.wording: Infants with screen positive results following NIPE infant 6 to 8-week screening examination should be referred directly to paediatric orthopaedic surgeon for urgent expert opinion and be seen by 10 weeks of age.

pass: First paediatric orthopaedic appointment attended on or before 70 days of age.
population: Infants referred after a screen-positive hip result at the 6–8 week GP check. Exclude infants already under the newborn hip pathway.
sample: All referrals over the last 12 months (expect 20–40).
data_source: e-Referral/outpatient system (referral date, triage, appointment); clinic letters; RIS (ultrasound).

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Create an e-Referral triage category 'NIPE 6–8 week hip – see by 10 weeks' that shows the date-of-birth-based deadline to the vetting consultant and books into a reserved slot.
reaudit: At 6 months: all referrals since the change, same template.
close_loop: Present to the screening board, GP leads and orthopaedic outpatients. If it works, write the category into the local NIPE pathway and inform GPs.
evidence: [1435] Glasgow: 56% → 76% (proforma prompt at the screening check)
[1527] Aberdeen: dedicated acute clinic halved time to surgery (system change)
effort: ~10 min per 10 infants from outpatient system
